question: You order sushi with vegetables or cooked seafood instead of raw fish. What still makes it sushi?
note: Sushi rice is dressed with vinegar, often with sugar and salt. Raw fish is one possible accompaniment, rather than the ingredient that every version must contain.

question: Ramen is now a worldwide symbol of Japanese food. Where do its noodle roots lead?
note: Ramen developed in Japan from Chinese-style wheat noodles. A food can become closely identified with one country while carrying a history of travel and adaptation.

question: Crisp tempura feels thoroughly Japanese, but visitors from which European country influenced its development?
note: Portuguese visitors helped introduce the style of frying that developed into tempura several centuries ago. By the Edo period, it was being sold from street stalls as a quick meal. Even the little scraps of fried batter have a use, becoming crunchy additions to noodle dishes.

question: The name oyakodon means “parent-and-child bowl.” Which ingredients explain it?
note: The parent is the chicken and the child is the egg, served together over rice. The name turns an ordinary combination into a small family joke.

question: A successful 1970s campaign helped turn which takeaway into a Christmas tradition for many people in Japan?
note: KFC launched its “Kentucky for Christmas” campaign in Japan in 1974. The promotion grew into a seasonal custom—a reminder that traditions can begin in an advertising department.

question: Beans do not have to be savoury. What is the classic filling in Japan’s dorayaki, a pair of small pancakes?
note: Azuki beans are cooked into a sweet paste and sandwiched between two small pancakes. Beans can play a dessert role as comfortably as a savoury one.

question: Japanese curry has Indian roots, but through which country did it reach Japan in the nineteenth century?
note: Curry reached Japan through Britain, which had already adapted dishes from India. Its journey did not simply go straight from one neighbouring Asian cuisine to another.

question: What did instant-noodle inventor Momofuku Ando see American buyers do that helped inspire Cup Noodles?
choices: Prepare and eat the noodles in cups
Toast the dry noodles like breakfast cereal
Wrap the noodles in bread to make sandwiches
Blend the noodles into a drink
note: The buyers broke noodles into cups, added hot water and ate them with forks. Ando saw that changing the container could help his Japanese invention fit a different way of eating.

question: When you drink matcha, what happens to the green tea leaves?
choices: You drink them as a fine powder mixed into the water
They are strained out after a very long steep
They are squeezed for juice and then discarded
note: Matcha is finely powdered green tea whisked into water. A bamboo whisk helps blend the powder instead of removing it as spent leaves.

question: A perfect bowl of noodles sits in a Japanese restaurant window all day without changing. What is it likely to be?
choices: A real meal kept frozen behind the glass
A dish coated in edible preserving jelly
A real meal replaced every few minutes
note: Many restaurants display remarkably lifelike models of their dishes. The models turn a menu into something you can see before ordering, without needing to know the name of every dish.

question: A museum calls its subject “Edo-Tokyo”. What is the relationship between those two names?
choices: They name the same city at different times
They are two cities joined into one capital
One names the city and the other its river
One is the city’s name and the other its ruling family
note: Edo was renamed Tokyo in 1868 as Japan entered a new political era. The museum’s name lets you travel through the history of one city, from the shoguns’ seat to the modern capital.

question: The word “geisha” literally points to an “arts person”. What is central to the profession?
choices: Caring for a shrine and conducting its rites
note: Geisha train in traditional performing arts and the skills of hosting guests. Their striking appearance is only the visible part of a profession built on years of artistic practice.

question: Deer roam freely around Nara’s famous shrine and park. What belief helped give them this special status?
choices: They are regarded as divine messengers
They are believed to be the emperor’s ancestors
They are thought to predict the rice harvest
They traditionally guide pilgrims to mountain summits
note: The deer’s religious association helps explain their protected place in the city. Visitors now know them for roaming the park and approaching people with deer crackers.

question: Engineers looked to a diving kingfisher when redesigning a Japanese bullet train’s nose. What were they trying to reduce?
choices: The boom produced when trains pass through tunnels
The glare of headlights reflected from the rails
The vibration caused by passengers walking
The heat produced when the brakes engage
note: A kingfisher moves from air into water with little splash. Engineer Eiji Nakatsu used that observation to help shape a train nose that handled pressure changes more quietly.

question: Mount Fuji looks peaceful in postcards. Which description is geologically correct?
choices: It is still classified as an active volcano
It is an extinct volcano with no volcanic activity possible
It is a mountain formed entirely by folded rock
It is a giant pile of rock left by a glacier
note: Fuji last erupted in 1707, but it is still classed as active. The long quiet interval and the familiar snow-covered silhouette can hide that volcanic identity.

question: Japan’s first bullet-train line opened just before a major event brought the world’s attention to Tokyo. Which event?
note: The Tokyo–Shin-Osaka service began on 1 October 1964. The new railway and the Olympics brought two lasting images of modern Japan into view together.

question: Sapporo’s enormous snow festival started with six sculptures. Who made those first creations?
note: Students made six snow sculptures in Odori Park in 1950. A modest local event grew into the festival associated with the city today.

question: Karate’s name means “empty hand”. What does that tell you about the martial art?
choices: The body is used without a handheld weapon
Only open palms may be used
A match begins with both hands on the floor
note: Karate developed in Okinawa through local traditions and Chinese influences before spreading across Japan. Its familiar name points to weaponless practice, rather than to a particular punch.

question: The red gates lining Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari shrine paths carry inscriptions. What do many of them record?
choices: The names of donors and donation dates
The names of rulers buried beneath them
The names of visiting foreign dignitaries
The names of the forest’s oldest trees
note: Individuals and businesses donate torii gates to the shrine. The famous paths are also a visible record of those contributions.

question: Miyajima’s huge shrine gate appears to stand in the sea. What mainly keeps it upright?
choices: Bolts fixing it to a stone base
Steel cables tied to the shore
note: The great torii stands under its own enormous weight rather than on pillars driven into the seabed. Stones packed into its upper beam add weight; at low tide, the water retreats from around its feet.

question: Washington, D.C.’s famous cherry blossoms have a Japanese connection. What brought thousands of the trees there in 1912?
choices: A gift of friendship from Tokyo
An order from an American fruit-growing company
A shipment intended for a Japanese temple
A prize awarded at an international gardening contest
note: Tokyo’s gift helped create one of Washington’s best-known spring landscapes. A familiar Japanese seasonal pleasure became a lasting part of another country’s capital.

question: “Emoji” sounds as though it comes from “emotion”. What do its Japanese parts actually mean?
note: The word combines e, meaning picture, with moji, meaning a written character. The resemblance to the English word “emotion” is a coincidence, even though emoji often communicate feelings.

question: On Children’s Day, Japanese families fly streamers shaped like carp. What hope does the fish express?
choices: They express hopes for strength and perseverance
They ask for a plentiful fishing season
They commemorate the start of spring planting
note: A legend tells of a carp overcoming a waterfall and becoming a dragon. The streamers turn that image of effort into a wish for children.

question: In a Japanese seasonal ritual, families throw beans to drive out demons. What are they symbolically making room for?
choices: A new household deity chosen each year
note: The ritual marks the seasonal turn before spring in the traditional calendar. A family member may wear a demon mask, making the symbolic eviction a household event.

question: At the lowered entrance area of a Japanese home, what does a visitor normally do before stepping inside?
choices: Put on a coat over their clothes
Wash their hands in the entrance basin
Wait for the host to ring a bell
note: The genkan separates outdoor footwear from indoor floors. The custom is especially practical where people sit or sleep close to the floor.

question: The size of a traditional Japanese room is often described by counting what?
note: Tatami mats are both flooring and a familiar measure of room size, though mat dimensions vary. A room described as “six mats” turns a floor covering into a unit of space.

question: In many Japanese schools, who regularly takes a turn cleaning the classrooms?
note: Classes divide cleaning duties among pupils, who sweep, wipe and tidy together. Looking after the shared room becomes part of the school day, rather than just something that happens after everyone leaves.

question: Japan’s compact capsule hotels originally offered a practical answer to which everyday problem?
choices: Needing to quarantine after overseas travel
Finding a room large enough for a whole family
Storing luggage during a short station stop
note: Early capsule hotels catered to workers needing an affordable overnight stay. A bed-sized private compartment and shared facilities turned a missed train into a manageable night away from home.

question: A Japanese daruma goal-setting doll often starts with only one painted eye. When is the second eye filled in?
note: The unpainted eye keeps an unfinished ambition visible. When the goal is achieved, completing the face turns private progress into a little ceremony.

question: The little cat with a raised paw often seen in Japanese shops can look as though it is waving goodbye. What is it actually doing?
note: The maneki-neko is beckoning, welcoming customers or good fortune. The same hand movement can look different to someone used to beckoning with the palm facing upwards.

question: The Tale of Genji was written about a thousand years ago. Who created this landmark of Japanese literature?
choices: A woman serving at the imperial court
A Buddhist monk writing in a monastery
A warrior recording life in a castle
note: The writer is known as Murasaki Shikibu, a woman at the imperial court. A major work of Japanese literature came from her observation of courtly life, centuries before the modern novel.

question: Look past the enormous wave in Hokusai’s famous print: which Japanese landmark appears small in the distance?
note: The wave dominates the image, but Fuji is part of its composition. The print belongs to Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji and uses the imported pigment Prussian blue.

question: How can an actor in Japanese Noh theatre make a rigid mask seem to change expression?
choices: By changing its angle and the way they move
By inflating small air pockets behind its cheeks
By pulling strings attached to its eyebrows
By changing its colour with body heat
note: Small changes in a mask’s angle can change how its expression is perceived. Noh brings mask, movement, voice and music together.

question: An English edition of a Japanese manga seems to open at the “back”. Why might the publisher have kept it that way?
choices: To preserve the original right-to-left reading order
To separate the pictures from the dialogue
To place the ending before a long flashback
To make the book easier to hold with one hand
note: Many translated manga preserve the Japanese arrangement of pages and panels. What looks backwards to an English-language reader is the original reading direction.

question: Kabuki is associated with male performers, including men in female roles. Who helped begin the form?
choices: A group of samurai performing for their ruler
A religious order presenting sacred dramas
A company adapting Chinese puppet plays
note: Izumo no Okuni performed in Kyoto in the early seventeenth century. Women were later banned from the public stage, changing who could perform the tradition.

question: Which origami bird became a powerful symbol of hope and peace, especially through the story of Hiroshima child Sadako Sasaki?
note: Sadako folded paper cranes while ill with leukaemia after surviving the atomic bombing as a young child. Cranes are still offered at the Children’s Peace Monument; she folded more than a thousand, despite a popular version saying she never reached that number.

question: What keeps a bonsai tree small?
choices: Careful pruning and training of an ordinary tree
Seeds from a naturally miniature tree species
A permanently dormant stage before adulthood
A special soil that stops all new growth
note: Bonsai are generally ordinary trees shaped through long-term care, including pruning roots and branches. The miniature landscape is a cultivated result, not a separate species of tiny tree.

question: A broken Japanese bowl is repaired using kintsugi. What happens to its cracks?
choices: They become visible lines highlighted with gold
They are hidden under a new glaze over the whole bowl
They are covered by carving a pattern into the surface
They disappear when the clay is fired again
note: Lacquer holds the fragments together and gold highlights the seams. Related repair techniques use silver or lacquer alone; in each case, repair can become part of the object’s appearance.

question: A historical ninja needed to gather information without attracting attention. Which outfit would fit that job?
choices: The clothes of an ordinary travelling merchant
A distinctive black uniform worn in every situation
A warrior’s armour displaying their employer’s crest
Ceremonial robes identifying them as a royal messenger
note: Ninja manuals describe disguises such as merchants, priests and performers. Looking like someone with an ordinary reason to travel could be more useful than looking like the ninja of a film.

question: Japanese art helped reshape Van Gogh’s painting. How did he get to know its visual world?
choices: Through Japanese prints imported into Europe
During a long painting trip through Japan
Through training at a Japanese art school
By sharing a studio with Japanese printmakers in Arles
note: Japanese woodblock prints helped change his use of colour and composition. His idea of Japan was partly an imagined one, formed through pictures rather than a visit.

question: According to Pac-Man’s creator, what meal helped inspire the character’s round shape and open mouth?
choices: A pizza with a slice missing
A doughnut with a hole in the middle
A bowl of rice with chopsticks across it
A sandwich cut into two triangles
note: Toru Iwatani described seeing the shape in a partly eaten pizza. A game about eating acquired a hero whose silhouette could itself be found on a dinner plate.

question: The original Godzilla reached cinemas in 1954. Which anxiety helped shape its destructive monster?
choices: The possibility of invasion from space
note: The black-and-white film was made after nuclear war and amid hydrogen-bomb testing in the Pacific. Its monster story carried fears that were very close to contemporary life.

question: What did Nintendo originally make when it was founded in 1889?
note: Nintendo began in Kyoto making hanafuda playing cards in 1889. Its business was already games, but its first players did not need a screen.

question: Which childhood pastime helped inspire Pokémon’s creator to make a game about finding and collecting creatures?
note: Satoshi Tajiri grew up exploring ponds and fields around his home. As those places disappeared under development, Pokémon offered children another world in which to discover and collect creatures.

question: Hello Kitty is a Japanese creation. In Sanrio’s fictional biography, where was she born?
note: Sanrio places Kitty White’s birth in suburban London. The global icon’s invented biography is British, even though the company that created her is Japanese.

question: Why did the original Mario get such a prominent moustache and a hat?
choices: They made his face readable with very few pixels
They copied the appearance of the designer’s father
They matched the uniform of a company sponsoring the game
They identified him as a villain in the original story
note: Designer Shigeru Miyamoto explained that the moustache saved the need to draw a mouth, while the hat simplified the hair. Technical limits helped create one of the most recognisable faces in games.

question: Before a sumo bout, a wrestler may throw salt into the ring. What is the ritual meant to do?
choices: Signal a challenge to the referee
note: The salt belongs to sumo’s ritual preparation and expresses a wish for safety in a purified ring. Some of the ceremony around a bout lasts longer than the wrestling itself.

question: Baseball’s Japanese history began well before the post-war American occupation. Who introduced it to students in 1872?
choices: An American teacher working in Japan
A Japanese emperor returning from a tour
A touring team of Hollywood actors
A British naval officer stationed in Tokyo
note: Teacher Horace Wilson introduced the game to his students in the nineteenth century. Japan’s deep baseball culture therefore has roots far older than the television era or post-war occupation.

question: Judo is often translated as “the gentle way”. How can that idea make sense in a sport full of throws?
choices: Using an opponent’s force and lost balance
Avoiding all physical contact during a contest
Moving as slowly as possible before each throw
Awarding victory to whoever uses the least time
note: The principle includes yielding and redirecting an opponent’s effort instead of simply opposing it. “Gentle” points to an approach to force, rather than a promise that nobody will hit the mat.

question: The word karaoke combines Japanese words meaning what?
note: Kara means “empty,” and oke is a shortening of okesutora, the Japanese borrowing of “orchestra.” The name describes an accompaniment that leaves room for the participant’s voice.
